tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success depends of careful planning before the launch.
She is responsible of the quarterly budget review.
They are interested on the revised merger proposal.
Despite of the delay, the audit was completed on time.
The firm was accused of misleading retail investors.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "depends on," not "depends of," for this fixed dependency pattern.

Tip: After "depend," lock in "on" — "of" is a common L1 transfer trap.

FALSE — Use "responsible for," not "responsible of."

Tip: Pair "responsible" with "for" + noun/gerund; "of" is wrong here.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is "interested in," not "interested on."

Tip: Interest takes "in"; "on" belongs with focus/concentrate.

FALSE — "Despite" never takes "of"; write "Despite the delay" or "In spite of the delay."

Tip: "Despite of" is always wrong — drop "of" or switch to "in spite of."

TRUE — "Accused of" + gerund/noun is the standard legal collocation.

Tip: Accuse/charge of wrongdoing; do not swap in "for" after "accused."
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each sentence for a fixed verb/adjective + preposition lock. Ask whether the preposition matches the standard pattern, and watch for the classic "despite of" false friend. Correct any mismatch before you mark TRUE.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He insisted on seeing the raw sales data.
The outcome differs of last year's forecast.
We apologised about the shipping delay to the client.
The report focuses to cost control measures.
She participated in the compliance workshop.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Insist on" + gerund is the fixed pattern here.

Tip: After "insist," use "on" + -ing, not a bare infinitive.

FALSE — Use "differs from," not "differs of."

Tip: Differ/different → from; do not write "differ of."

FALSE — Prefer "apologised for the shipping delay" in careful exam English.

Tip: Apologise for a fault or inconvenience; "about" is weaker and often marked wrong.

FALSE — Use "focuses on," not "focuses to."

Tip: Focus/concentrate take "on," never "to."

TRUE — "Participated in" correctly names involvement in an event.

Tip: Participate/join/engage → in an event or activity.
tasks.solution_overview: These items test high-frequency business collocations. Match each verb to its locked preposition, and rewrite any false friend before deciding TRUE or FALSE.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They objected against the indemnity clause.
The consultant is capable of handling the negotiation.
Managers must be aware of the new disclosure rules.
She is good in presenting quarterly results.
We look forward to receiving your comments.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "objected to the clause," not "against."

Tip: Object to X; "against" belongs with protest/argue in other patterns.

TRUE — "Capable of" + gerund is correct.

Tip: Capable/incapable take "of," not "to."

TRUE — "Aware of" correctly introduces the known fact or risk.

Tip: Aware/conscious → of; "about" is looser and often weaker in exams.

FALSE — Say "good at presenting," not "good in."

Tip: Good/bad/skilled → at + -ing for ability.

TRUE — "Look forward to" + gerund is fixed; "to" is a preposition here.

Tip: After "look forward to," keep -ing, never a bare infinitive.
tasks.solution_overview: Adjective and verb patterns lock specific prepositions. Check whether "of," "to," "at," or "in" is the required partner, especially after capable, aware, good, and look forward.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The project succeeded in cutting overhead by eight percent.
The package consists of three separate modules.
The forecast is based on conservative assumptions.
These findings are related to last quarter's results.
According with the auditor, the controls are adequate.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Succeed in" + gerund names the achievement.

Tip: Succeed in doing X; do not write "succeed to do."

TRUE — "Consists of" correctly lists the parts.

Tip: Consist of / be composed of — never "from" after consist.

TRUE — "Based on" correctly introduces the foundation of the claim.

Tip: Base/based → on evidence or assumptions.

TRUE — "Related to" is the fixed comparison/link pattern.

Tip: Related/similar → to; "with" is a common trap after related.

FALSE — Use "According to the auditor," not "according with."

Tip: According to + person/document; never "according with" for this meaning.
tasks.solution_overview: Report-writing English leans on a small set of locked phrases. Verify each preposition against the standard business pattern before you accept the sentence.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deputy is in charge of the regional rollout.
Investors rely on timely disclosures from management.
The team must deal with customer complaints promptly.
Nothing will prevent us from meeting the deadline.
Higher rates resulted in weaker loan demand.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "In charge of" correctly marks responsibility for a domain.

Tip: In charge of X ≈ responsible for X.

TRUE — "Rely on" is the fixed dependency pattern.

Tip: Rely/depend → on; both reject "of" in exam English.

TRUE — "Deal with" correctly introduces the problem handled.

Tip: Deal with a problem or person; "about" does not replace "with" here.

TRUE — "Prevent … from" + gerund is correct.

Tip: Prevent/stop/discourage someone from doing X.

TRUE — Outcomes "result in" an effect; that direction is right here.

Tip: Result in = cause → effect; result from = effect ← cause.
tasks.solution_overview: These workplace phrases are almost mechanical once you know the lock. Confirm each verb/adjective still carries its standard preposition before marking TRUE.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Our approach is similar to the peer group's model.
This year's margin is different than last year's by a wide gap.
The campaign aims for increasing brand recognition only.
She is dedicated for improving internal controls.
New hires quickly became accustomed to remote tools.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Similar to" is the standard comparison pattern.

Tip: Similar to X; "with" is wrong after similar.

FALSE — Careful exam English prefers "different from" (or "different to" in some BrE), not "different than" in this frame.

Tip: On WU-style papers, choose "different from" and avoid "than" after different.

FALSE — Prefer "aims at increasing" or "aims to increase," not "aims for increasing."

Tip: Aim at / aim to are the safe exam pairs; "aim for" usually takes a noun goal.

FALSE — Use "dedicated to improving," not "for."

Tip: Dedicated/committed/devoted → to + -ing.

TRUE — "Accustomed to" correctly marks the habit pattern.

Tip: Accustomed/used → to; "with" is a frequent trap.
tasks.solution_overview: Comparison and attitude adjectives often lock "to" or "from." Read past the content words and test only the preposition that follows the key adjective.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board congratulated her for completing the turnaround.
Staff complained about the abrupt schedule change.
Please apply to the vacancy before Friday.
They applied for the graduate scheme in June.
The memo refers on last week's minutes.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Congratulate someone for/on" an achievement both occur; "for completing" is acceptable here.

Tip: Congratulate + person + for/on + achievement.

TRUE — "Complain about" correctly names the grievance.

Tip: Complain about X; complain to a person.

FALSE — Jobs and schemes take "apply for"; "apply to" targets an organisation or address.

Tip: Apply for a post; apply to a company/university.

TRUE — "Applied for the graduate scheme" is the correct job-application pattern.

Tip: For + what you want; to + who receives the application.

FALSE — Use "refers to last week's minutes," not "refers on."

Tip: Refer to a document or point; "on" belongs with focus/comment in other patterns.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply/refer/complain change meaning with the preposition. Decide what the object is — a job, a person, or a document — then pick the locked partner.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The policy benefits from clearer wording.
Clients benefit from lower transaction fees.
We agreed on a revised delivery window.
They agreed with the supplier's new terms.
She insisted to reopen the closed account.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Benefit from" correctly marks the source of advantage.

Tip: Benefit from X; never "benefit of" as the verb pattern.

TRUE — Verb "benefit" takes "from" for the source of the gain.

Tip: "Be of benefit to" is a different structure — do not mix it with the verb.

TRUE — "Agree on" a plan, date, or figure is standard.

Tip: Agree on a thing; agree with a person/opinion.

TRUE — "Agree with" the supplier's terms correctly accepts another's position.

Tip: With + person/opinion; on + joint decision.

FALSE — Use "insisted on reopening," not "insisted to reopen."

Tip: Insist on + -ing; the infinitive after insist is a classic trap.
tasks.solution_overview: Small preposition swaps change meaning or break the pattern entirely. Separate "agree on" from "agree with," and keep gerunds after "insist on."

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite the headwinds, revenue still grew.
Despite of rising costs, margins held steady.
She disapproves against remote-only onboarding.
The committee approved against the contingency plan.
Despite the headwinds, revenue still grew.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "In spite" must be followed by "of"; write "In spite of the headwinds."

Tip: In spite of = despite; never drop of from the three-word phrase.

FALSE — "Despite of" is ungrammatical; drop "of" or use "in spite of."

Tip: If you hear "of," the safe rewrite is "in spite of."

FALSE — Use "disapproves of," not "against."

Tip: Approve/disapprove of X; "against" belongs with be/argue.

FALSE — Use "approved of the plan" (attitude) or "approved the plan" (formal decision) — not "against."

Tip: Approve of an idea; do not invent "approve against."

TRUE — "Despite" + noun phrase is correct and needs no "of."

Tip: Despite ≠ despite of — never add "of" after despite.
tasks.solution_overview: Concession phrases and approval verbs are frequent exam traps. Confirm that "despite" stands alone, that "in spite of" keeps its of, and that approve/disapprove take "of" when an attitude is meant.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The delay was due to a supplier outage.
Owing to the outage, shipments slipped by two days.
Because of the outage last Tuesday, filings slipped.
He was blamed for the reporting error.
In spite of the outage, the team filed on time.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Due to" + noun correctly states the cause after a linking verb.

Tip: Due to / owing to + noun; not + bare clause.

TRUE — "Owing to" + noun is a formal cause marker.

Tip: Owing to ≈ because of; both need a noun phrase.

TRUE — "Because of" + noun correctly marks the cause.

Tip: Because + clause; because of + noun.

TRUE — "Blamed for" an error is the fixed responsibility pattern.

Tip: Blame someone for X; be blamed for X — not "of."

TRUE — "In spite of" + noun is the complete three-word concession phrase.

Tip: Mirror check: if despite works, in spite of should too — with of included.
tasks.solution_overview: Cause and concession patterns look similar but lock different partners. Check that due to/owing to/because of take nouns, and keep blamed for distinct from accused of.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The analyst is familiar with the IFRS disclosure notes.
Few staff are familiar to the new CRM workflow.
He specialised in cross-border tax structuring.
The firm specialises on logistics software.
We must comply to the updated privacy regulation.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Familiar with" correctly marks knowledge of a topic.

Tip: Familiar with X; "to" belongs with "familiar to someone" in a different frame.

FALSE — People are "familiar with" a system; a system can be "familiar to" people — here you need "with."

Tip: Subject = person → familiar with; subject = thing → familiar to + person.

TRUE — "Specialise in" a field is the fixed pattern.

Tip: Specialise/major → in a subject area.

FALSE — Use "specialises in," not "on."

Tip: On appears with focus/concentrate; specialise stays with in.

FALSE — Use "comply with" a regulation, not "comply to."

Tip: Comply with rules; never "comply to" on careful papers.
tasks.solution_overview: Expertise and compliance language uses a narrow set of prepositions. Watch the familiar with/to swap and keep specialise/comply on their locked partners.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The warranty covers damage resulting from misuse.
Better training resulted in fewer service tickets.
The shortage resulted of a warehouse fire.
They congratulated the team on winning the tender.
Please comment the draft before noon.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Resulting from" correctly marks the cause of the damage.

Tip: Result from = come from a cause.

TRUE — "Resulted in" correctly marks the effect produced.

Tip: Result in = lead to an outcome.

FALSE — Causes take "resulted from," not "of."

Tip: Never write "result of" as a verb pattern; "be the result of" is a noun pattern.

TRUE — "Congratulate … on" an achievement is fully standard.

Tip: On/for both appear after congratulate; on + -ing is very common.

FALSE — You "comment on the draft," not "comment the draft" in this exam register.

Tip: Comment on / make comments on a document.
tasks.solution_overview: Result in vs result from is a direction test: effect versus cause. Finish by checking whether transitive-looking verbs still need a preposition, as with comment on.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The CFO is committed to reducing leverage this year.
They are opposed to selling the subsidiary now.
She is keen on expanding into adjacent markets.
He is keen in expanding into adjacent markets.
We are accustomed to filing reports every Friday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Committed to" + gerund shows firm intention.

Tip: To after committed/dedicated is a preposition, so -ing follows.

TRUE — "Opposed to" + gerund correctly states resistance.

Tip: Opposed to X / to doing X — keep the gerund.

TRUE — "Keen on" + gerund is the usual BrE ability/interest pattern.

Tip: Keen on -ing; keen to + infinitive is a different but also valid frame.

FALSE — Not "keen in"; use "keen on" or "keen to."

Tip: In does not partner with keen for this meaning.

TRUE — "Accustomed to" + gerund matches the fixed habit pattern.

Tip: Accustomed/used to + -ing (prepositional to).
tasks.solution_overview: Attitude adjectives followed by "to" or "on" still take gerunds because that "to" is a preposition. Reject any swap that inserts "in" where "on" or "to" is locked.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nothing will stop the bank from raising its forecast.
The clause prohibits staff from sharing client files externally.
Higher volumes translated into stronger fee income.
The discussion centred on pricing strategy.
Investors look forward to hearing the revised guidance.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Stop … from" + gerund is correct.

Tip: Stop/prevent/keep someone from doing X.

TRUE — "Prohibits … from sharing" is the fixed pattern.

Tip: Prohibit/ban/discourage from -ing — not to + infinitive.

TRUE — "Translate into" an outcome is a standard figurative collocation.

Tip: Translate into = result in; "to" is weaker here.

TRUE — "Centred on" correctly names the topic focus.

Tip: Centre/focus/concentrate → on a topic.

TRUE — "Look forward to" + gerund remains fixed in formal updates.

Tip: After look forward to, keep -ing because to is a preposition.
tasks.solution_overview: Restriction verbs almost always take "from" + gerund. Pair that with topic verbs that lock "on," and you can clear most of this set quickly.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whether we expand depends of next quarter's cash flow.
He takes pride of mentoring junior analysts.
The review will take account to seasonal effects.
She was blamed of the reporting error.
The bonus depends on whether targets are met.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Still "depends on," even before a clause — never "of."

Tip: The clause after depend does not change the locked preposition.

FALSE — Not "pride of"; that mixes "proud of" with "take pride in."

Tip: Keep the pairs intact: pride in ≠ proud of.

FALSE — Use "take account of," not "to."

Tip: Take account of X; take into account is the sibling pattern.

FALSE — Not "blamed of"; that pattern belongs with accused/suspected.

Tip: Blamed for ≠ accused of — keep the pairs separate.

TRUE — "Depend on whether…" correctly introduces a condition.

Tip: Depend on + noun/whether-clause; the preposition stays "on."
tasks.solution_overview: Fixed phrases stay fixed even when a clause follows. Watch for crossed pairs such as pride in vs proud of, and keep "depend on" through every continuation.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The recommendation rests on three independent studies.
Their case rests in three independent studies.
We cannot dispense with the interim audit this year.
The plan provides for a mid-year stress test.
The plan provides of a mid-year stress test.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Rest on" evidence or assumptions is correct.

Tip: Rest on / be based on — both take "on."

FALSE — Use "rests on," not "in," for this meaning.

Tip: In would suggest location; the argumentative sense needs on.

TRUE — "Dispense with" (= do without) is a fixed formal pattern.

Tip: Dispense with X; do not invent "dispense of."

TRUE — "Provide for" a contingency means make arrangements for it.

Tip: Provide for = make provision; provide someone with = supply.

FALSE — Not "provides of"; use "provides for" or "provides … with."

Tip: Of after provide is almost always wrong in exam English.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal report verbs hide fixed prepositions. Rest on, dispense with, and provide for each lock one partner — treat any other preposition as a trap.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The board will not enter into a binding commitment yet.
They entered in negotiations without legal counsel.
Investors put pressure on management to clarify guidance.
The delay put pressure to the operations team.
She was charged for insider trading last month.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Enter into" an agreement or commitment is the formal pattern.

Tip: Enter into a contract/talks; enter a room needs no into.

FALSE — Negotiations take "entered into," not "entered in."

Tip: For abstract agreements and talks, keep into.

TRUE — "Put pressure on" someone is fixed.

Tip: Pressure on a person/organisation; not "to" the person.

FALSE — Use "put pressure on the operations team," not "to."

Tip: On marks the target of pressure; to marks direction elsewhere.

FALSE — Use "charged with" an offence, not "for."

Tip: Charged with ≈ accused of; keep each pair as learned.
tasks.solution_overview: Legal and negotiation English mixes "enter into," "charged with," and "pressure on." These are memorised locks — if the preposition feels improvised, it is probably wrong.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The division accounts for nearly forty percent of revenue.
Poor controls accounted to several reporting breaches.
We must allow for currency swings in the model.
The schedule does not allow of further slippage.
Despite the fact that costs rose, cash flow improved.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Account for" a share or proportion is correct.

Tip: Account for = constitute / explain.

FALSE — Explanations also "account for" events — not "account to."

Tip: Account to someone = report to them; account for something = explain it.

TRUE — "Allow for" a risk means include it in planning.

Tip: Allow for = make provision for.

TRUE — Formal "allow of" (= permit) is rare but grammatical in this sense.

Tip: Allow of = admit the possibility of; different from allow for.

TRUE — "Despite the fact that" correctly introduces a full clause after despite.

Tip: Despite + noun, or despite the fact that + clause — still no "despite of."
tasks.solution_overview: Account for vs account to, and allow for vs allow of, are advanced pairs with different meanings. Read for sense, then confirm the preposition matches that sense — including the legal "despite the fact that" workaround.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee insisted that the clause be revised, and the lawyer insisted on seeing the redraft.
She was suspected of leaking the memo to the press.
The flotation went ahead in spite of the delays.
She takes pride in mentoring junior analysts.
Notwithstanding the objections, the board adopted the policy.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Two different "insist" patterns can coexist: subjunctive that-clause, and "insist on" + gerund.

Tip: Insist that + base form ≠ insist on + -ing — both are fixed, but they are not interchangeable.

TRUE — "Suspected of" + gerund is the legal collocation.

Tip: Suspected/accused/convicted of wrongdoing.

TRUE — "In spite of the delays" is fully correct.

Tip: Mirror check: if despite works, in spite of should too — with of included.

TRUE — "Take pride in" + gerund is fixed.

Tip: Pride in / proud of — different heads, different prepositions.

TRUE — "Notwithstanding" works like despite and takes a noun phrase with no extra of.

Tip: Notwithstanding X ≈ despite X; do not write "notwithstanding of."
tasks.solution_overview: High-band items mix near-identical frames correctly. Separate insist that from insist on, keep suspected of and pride in, and leave notwithstanding without a trailing of.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Please refrain to call the client until legal has cleared the script.
The bonus pool is contingent of meeting group targets.
She was suspected for leaking the memo to the press.
In spite the delays, the flotation went ahead.
The lenders will refrain from calling the loan if covenants hold.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Not "refrain to call"; use "refrain from calling."

Tip: From + -ing after refrain/abstain.

FALSE — Use "contingent on," not "of."

Tip: Of after contingent is a depend-of style transfer error.

FALSE — Use "suspected of," not "for."

Tip: Suspected/accused of wrongdoing — keep for for blame.

FALSE — "In spite" must be followed by "of"; "in spite the delays" is incomplete.

Tip: In spite of = despite; never drop of from the three-word phrase.

TRUE — "Refrain from" + gerund is the fixed restraint pattern.

Tip: Refrain from doing X; never a bare infinitive after refrain.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with formal restraint and condition traps. Refrain from and contingent on behave like depend on; strip away every false of/for/to before accepting a sentence.
